Lessons.Title: Number Puzzles
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret a verbal number puzzle as an equation, define an unknown and test a solution by substitution.

Translate each clue into a relationship; a phrase such as “twice a number plus three equals fifteen” means 2x+3=15, while “twice the sum of a number and three” would mean 2(x+3). Parentheses reflect the meaning.

Create two original number puzzles for classmates, exchange them, and check that each has a consistent solution. A teacher reviews the language-to-algebra translation and ambiguity, not just a numeric answer.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/1/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unknown number
KeyConcepts.Definition: A variable standing for an unspecified value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Write one equation consistent with every clue.
KeyConcepts.Example: If x is the number, twice it plus 3 is 2x+3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A statement of equality with mathematical expressions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Only a satisfying value is a solution.

KeyConcepts.Title: Verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: Substituting the proposed solution into the original puzzle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve a puzzle
WorkedExamples.Question: Twice a number plus three is fifteen. Find it.

WorkedExamples.Title: Different parentheses
WorkedExamples.Question: Twice the sum of a number and three is sixteen. Find it.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check a wrong guess
WorkedExamples.Question: For 3x−2=13, does x=4 work?
Steps: 10 differs from 13, so x=4 is not a solution.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Missing parentheses in a phrase about a sum.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 2x+3 is not the same as 2(x+3).

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting a guess without checking.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An equation solution must satisfy the original equality.

SummaryPoints: Define the unknown first.
Translate groups and operations exactly.
Verify a solution with substitution.

Lessons.Title: Keeping the Equation Balanced
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use a balanced hanger model to represent an equation and find unknown weights without disrupting equality.

Equal hanger arms carry equal total weight. If one object x appears on each arm, remove an equal quantity from both sides. When identical unknown bags occur together, dividing equally across bags determines the weight per bag.

Make an original picture with two identical bags and a three-unit weight balancing an eleven-unit weight. Interpret it as 2x+3=11. A teacher evaluates diagram alignment and explanation; one numerical result does not verify the physical model.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/2/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Balanced model
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two equal-weight sides of a hanger represent equal expressions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Apply the same permissible change to both sides.

KeyConcepts.Title: Remove equal weights
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtract the same quantity from each side.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equality remains valid after subtracting c from both.

KeyConcepts.Title: Share the remaining weight
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divide equal total weights across identical bags.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two-bag hanger
WorkedExamples.Question: Two equal bags plus three units balance eleven. Find each bag.
Steps: Subtract three units from both hanger arms.

WorkedExamples.Title: Three-bag hanger
WorkedExamples.Question: Three bags balance fifteen units. Find one bag.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject asymmetric removal
WorkedExamples.Question: If x+7=12, is x+7−7=12−3 a valid balance move?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare the operations on both sides.
Steps: Seven is removed from the left.
Three is removed from the right.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Removing weight from only one arm.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It destroys the equality of total weights.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Make each operation on both sides.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming bags can have arbitrary weights on one hanger.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Identically marked bags represent equal unknown weights.

SummaryPoints: Balanced hangers encode equations.
Maintain identical operations on both sides.
Verify bag weights by recomputing totals.

Visuals.Title: Which candidate balances 2x+3=11?
Visuals.Description: A solution has equal left and right sides; x=4 is the only solution shown.

Lessons.Title: Balanced Moves
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: rewrite equations with equivalent expressions while preserving exactly the same solution set.
Adding, subtracting, multiplying by a nonzero value or dividing by a nonzero value on both sides preserves equality. Distributing and combining like terms preserve an expression’s value.

Write two legal chains from 3x+5=20 to x=5. Exchange with a classmate and identify each operation. Written descriptions of equivalence need teacher judgment; a correct final answer alone is not full evidence.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/3/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent equations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equations with identical solution sets.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Apply reversible operations to both sides.

KeyConcepts.Title: Balance operations
KeyConcepts.Definition: The same addition/subtraction or nonzero scaling on both sides.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep both expressions equal at every step.

KeyConcepts.Title: Identity substitution check
KeyConcepts.Definition: A proposed answer must satisfy original and transformed equations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject one-sided change
WorkedExamples.Question: A learner changes x+4=9 to x=9. Is this equivalent?
Steps: The two equations have different solutions.
WorkedExamples.Check: Subtract four on both sides to get x=5.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Cancelling a term from only one side.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It changes the solution set.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing by zero.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That is not a valid reversible operation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Only divide by a demonstrated nonzero number.

SummaryPoints: Equivalent equations preserve solutions.
Reversible balanced steps are justified.
Check transformed and original equalities.

Lessons.Title: More Balanced Moves
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use the distributive property, combining like terms and balanced operations to simplify equations with expressions on both sides.

When expressions occur on both sides, collect variable terms on one side and constants on the other. A move such as subtracting 2x from both sides is legal; dividing by a variable expression may not be reversible if that expression can equal zero.

Construct a diagram showing equal expressions 5x+2 and 2x+14. Explain how removing two x-tiles from both sides isolates the remaining three. A teacher reviews the algebraic diagram and validity of each step.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/4/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Combine like terms
KeyConcepts.Definition: Merge coefficients of the same variable.

KeyConcepts.Title: Variables on both sides
KeyConcepts.Definition: Keep equality while moving unknown terms.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Subtract a variable term from both sides.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distribution
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply each term inside parentheses.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating x+x as x².
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Repeated variable addition is coefficient addition.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Distributing to only the first term.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Every parenthesized term is multiplied.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a visual area model for each term.

SummaryPoints: Combine like terms accurately.
Balance both sides when moving terms.
Check the original equation after solving.

Visuals.Title: Variables on both sides
Visuals.Description: The two expressions equal each other only when x=4 among the candidates shown.

Lessons.Title: Solving Any Linear Equation
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use reliable symbolic strategies for one-variable affine equations with fractions or variables on both sides while recognizing exceptional solution counts.

A linear equation ax+b=cx+d can have one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions depending on the resulting coefficients. Operations must preserve its solution set, including multiplying by the common denominator when fractional coefficients occur.
Work a complete explanation rather than only a final numeric answer. A teacher assesses strategy clarity; numeric solutions can be independently checked against the original.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/5/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Affine equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Variables appear to first degree with constant coefficients.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Collect all x terms and constant terms.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unique solution
KeyConcepts.Definition: After simplification, nonzero multiple of x equals a number.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fraction clearing
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply both sides by a common nonzero denominator.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Preserves solutions when done on both sides.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dropping negative signs when dividing.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Sign determines solution direction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Clearing only one fraction term.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Multiplication applies to the entire equation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply both sides and all terms consistently.

SummaryPoints: Collect variable terms and constants.
Fractions and negative coefficients require careful balance.
Verification against the original guards mistakes.

Lessons.Title: Strategic Solving
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: choose an efficient order of legal operations to solve a linear equation without unnecessary expansion or arithmetic errors.

An equation with a factored expression can often be simplified by dividing first; another may benefit from distributing. Compare the number of steps and the potential for sign mistakes, then verify both strategies lead to the same answer.

Give students 4(x+3)=28 and ask them to solve in two ways, explain what is more economical, and critique a common distribution mistake. Teacher evaluation focuses on mathematical explanation rather than speed alone.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/6/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Factor-first strategy
KeyConcepts.Definition: Isolate a product before expanding.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If a(x+b)=c and a≠0, divide by a.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distribution strategy
KeyConcepts.Definition: Expand products when it helps collect terms.

KeyConcepts.Title: Efficiency check
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare correct solution paths while preserving equivalence.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rewarding a shortcut without justification.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Skipping necessary equal operations can conceal errors.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State why the shortcut preserves equality.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choosing distribution and losing a sign.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Every term inside must be multiplied.

SummaryPoints: Multiple equivalent solution paths are valid.
Choose steps that reduce errors.
Explain and verify the chosen strategy.

Lessons.Title: All, Some, or No Solutions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: distinguish equations true for all real x, true for exactly one x, and true for no x using equivalent transformations.
If simplifying yields 0=0, every x satisfies the original; if it yields 0=nonzero, none does. If it yields ax=b with a≠0, exactly one solution exists.

Sort original independently written equations into these three cases. A teacher reviews the explanation of why a statement is always or never true; test substitutions alone are insufficient to prove an identity.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/7/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Identity
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equation true for every real input.

KeyConcepts.Title: Contradiction
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equation false for every real input.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unique solution
KeyConcepts.Definition: A linear equation determining one x.

WorkedExamples.Title: Identity test
WorkedExamples.Question: How many solutions does 2(x+3)=2x+6 have?
Steps: Subtract to obtain 0=0, true for all real x.
WorkedExamples.Check: Any number makes both sides equal.

WorkedExamples.Title: Contradiction test
WorkedExamples.Question: How many solutions does 2x+1=2x+5 have?
WorkedExamples.Check: Both sides differ by 4 for every x.

WorkedExamples.Title: Unique case
WorkedExamples.Question: How many solutions does 2x+1=9 have?
Steps: Nonzero coefficient guarantees one real value.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming all linear equations have one solution.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The variable can cancel, leaving an identity or contradiction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a few sample values to prove all real x.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Finite tests cannot prove an identity.

SummaryPoints: Equation solution counts can be none, one, or infinitely many.
0=0 signals an identity.
0=nonzero signals contradiction.

Visuals.Title: Identity versus contradiction
Visuals.Description: The first equation is true for all real x; the second equation 2x+1=2x+5 is never true.

Lessons.Title: How Many Solutions?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: classify and explain the number of solutions of unfamiliar linear equations, including those with fractions and distribution.

Multiply or expand carefully, then inspect whether any nonzero x term remains. Two superficially different expressions can be identical after expansion. A different constant after cancellation indicates no solution.
Sort and justify three equations drawn from separately prepared cards. A teacher evaluates equivalent-transformation arguments rather than mere labels.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/8/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Coefficient comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare variable coefficients after simplification.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equal coefficients cancel; compare constants next.

KeyConcepts.Title: Identity detection
KeyConcepts.Definition: Every x works when expressions simplify identically.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unique detection
KeyConcepts.Definition: Remaining nonzero variable coefficient produces one solution.

WorkedExamples.Title: Contradiction with fractions
WorkedExamples.Question: Solutions to x/2+1=x/2+3?
Steps: No real x can satisfy this.
WorkedExamples.Check: The right side always exceeds the left by 2.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Stopping when variables cancel and saying “x=0.”
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A variable-free statement must be checked.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Expanding coefficients incorrectly.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Incorrect distribution changes solution count.

SummaryPoints: Solution count is an algebraic property.
Inspect the simplified constant statement.
A consistent coefficient comparison prevents guessing.

Lessons.Title: When Are They the Same?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: model when two quantities from different linear rules are equal and interpret the equation’s solution in a realistic context.
For two subscription plans, matching costs are found by setting the rules equal, not by comparing one arbitrary sample. The equality point can be shown on a graph as a line intersection.
Compare plan A at $6 plus $3 per month and plan B at $18 plus $1 per month. A teacher reviews what the break-even value means and whether fractional months are meaningful under the pricing rules.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/9/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Break-even equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equation formed by setting two models equal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Intersection meaning
KeyConcepts.Definition: Input where both outputs agree.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Same point lies on both graphs.

KeyConcepts.Title: Context domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: Only input values supported by the problem.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Months may be nonnegative whole counts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find equal costs
WorkedExamples.Question: Plan A is 6+3m and B is 18+m. When are they equal?

WorkedExamples.Title: Check a short period
WorkedExamples.Question: Which plan costs less after 2 months?

WorkedExamples.Title: Check a later period
WorkedExamples.Question: Which plan costs less after 10 months?
WorkedExamples.Check: After break-even, smaller monthly rate wins.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating only initial fees.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equal starting charges are not the same as equal total charges.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring feasible time intervals.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Negative months are not meaningful for this contract.

SummaryPoints: Two linear models are equal at a break-even input.
The equality appears as a graph intersection.
Interpret the solution in its domain.

Visuals.Title: Find the break-even month
Visuals.Description: Plan A=6+3m; plan B=18+m. They have equal price at month 6.

Lessons.Title: On or Off the Line?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret ordered pairs as solutions or nonsolutions of a contextual linear equation, and explain which points lie on its graph.

A point is on a line if its coordinates satisfy the equation exactly. A plotted point that merely looks close is not an exact solution. Negative values may be algebraically valid but contextually inappropriate.
Investigate a taxi fare F=4+2d. Sort points (0,4), (3,10), (3,11) by substitution and explain which are valid fare-distance combinations. A teacher checks graph reading and context.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/10/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: On-line test
KeyConcepts.Definition: Substitution makes the defining equation true.

KeyConcepts.Title: Off-line test
KeyConcepts.Definition: The ordered pair fails the equation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: An approximate graph dot is not enough.

KeyConcepts.Title: Context validity
KeyConcepts.Definition: The point must also make sense in the situation.
KeyConcepts.Example: (−2,0) satisfies equation but is not a realistic trip.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject an off-line point
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (3,11) on F=4+2d?
Steps: It does not satisfy the equation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Algebra versus context
WorkedExamples.Question: Does (−2,0) satisfy F=4+2d? Is it realistic?
WorkedExamples.Method: Separate equation check from physical interpretation.
Steps: A trip length cannot be negative, so the point is contextually invalid.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Judging graph membership by closeness of a hand drawing.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The graph is an exact solution set.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Conflating algebraic and context restrictions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A solution may violate domain assumptions.

SummaryPoints: Line points exactly satisfy the equation.
Nonmembers fail substitution.
Context may further restrict allowed solutions.

Lessons.Title: On Both of the Lines
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: identify an ordered pair that satisfies two line equations simultaneously and interpret this as the intersection of their graphs.
Two independent equations yield an intersection only where both balances hold. Testing a point in one line is insufficient; substitute into both.
Plot y=x+1 and y=−x+5, identify the intersection and explain its meaning in terms of equal outputs. The teacher reviews the coordinate graph and line intersection.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/11/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common solution
KeyConcepts.Definition: One ordered pair satisfying both linear equations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Intersection
KeyConcepts.Definition: A coordinate shared by two graph lines.

KeyConcepts.Title: Verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: A pair is common only if both substitutions are true.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject one-line point
WorkedExamples.Question: Does (0,1) lie on both y=x+1 and y=−x+5?
WorkedExamples.Check: One satisfied line does not make a common solution.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Checking only one equation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The system requires simultaneous truth.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming plotted lines meet exactly at a fuzzy grid point.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Hand plotting may be imprecise.

SummaryPoints: A shared solution lies on both lines.
Intersections can be computed by equal outputs.
Verify both equations.

Visuals.Title: Intersection of two lines
Visuals.Description: For the same x, both y-values agree at (2,3). A graph must be represented separately.

Lessons.Title: Systems of Equations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: understand a system of two linear equations as simultaneous constraints and classify possible intersections.

Two distinct nonparallel lines intersect once, parallel distinct lines have no common point, and coincident lines share infinitely many. A graph can illustrate these cases but exact equations establish which applies.
Use an original graph of y=2x+1 and y=2x−3 to explain no intersection, then compare y=2x+1 and 2y=4x+2. A teacher checks structural and graphical reasoning.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/12/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear system
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two or more equations required to hold simultaneously.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel distinct lines
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal slope but different intercepts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: They have no common ordered pair.

KeyConcepts.Title: Coincident lines
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different equations defining the same line.

WorkedExamples.Title: No intersection
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve y=2x+1 and y=2x−3.
WorkedExamples.Check: Distinct parallel lines have the same slope.

WorkedExamples.Title: Infinitely many
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve y=2x+1 and 2y=4x+2.
Steps: Every point on that line satisfies both.
WorkedExamples.Check: Two equations describe the same line.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a system as two separate unrelated answers.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The common solution must satisfy both.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming parallel lines always overlap.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Same slope with different intercepts gives distinct lines.

SummaryPoints: Systems encode simultaneous conditions.
Intersections can be zero, one or infinitely many.
Graph shape and algebra must agree.

Visuals.Title: Parallel and distinct equations
Visuals.Description: Two lines with slope 2 and different intercepts never intersect.

Lessons.Title: Solving Systems of Equations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: solve two-variable linear systems using substitution and verify the ordered-pair solution in both equations.
Choose substitution when one variable is already isolated. Replace that variable in the other equation, solve for the remaining variable, then back-substitute and check both originals.
Solve y=2x+1 together with x+y=10. Discuss whether a plotted approximation and an exact algebraic answer agree. A teacher reviews the substitution sequence.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/13/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Substitution
KeyConcepts.Definition: Replace an isolated variable by its equal expression.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If y=2x+1, use it in x+y=10.

KeyConcepts.Title: Back-substitution
KeyConcepts.Definition: Find the second coordinate once the first is known.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Insert solved x into either equation.

KeyConcepts.Title: System check
KeyConcepts.Definition: Test the ordered pair in both equations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject candidate
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (4,6) a solution to y=2x+1, x+y=10?
Steps: Since 6≠9, the point fails the system.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forgetting to distribute while substituting expressions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Parentheses may change signs and coefficients.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Checking only the equation used last.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An algebra slip can still produce an inconsistent pair.

SummaryPoints: Substitute an already isolated variable.
Back-substitute and obtain an ordered pair.
Check both equations.

Visuals.Title: Check both parts of a system
Visuals.Description: Only (3,7) satisfies y=2x+1 and x+y=10 in these choices.

Lessons.Title: Solving More Systems
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: choose an efficient substitution or elimination strategy for linear systems, including oppositely signed variable coefficients.

Elimination adds or subtracts equivalent equations to cancel one variable. You may multiply an entire equation by a nonzero constant first. An intersection must still be checked in the original system.
Use x+y=7 and x−y=1. Compare elimination with substitution and explain their equivalent solutions. A teacher reviews the justification for adding whole equations.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/14/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Elimination
KeyConcepts.Definition: Combine equations to remove one variable.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add equations when coefficients are opposites.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equation scaling
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply all terms by a nonzero constant.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common check
KeyConcepts.Definition: Verify the final pair in both original equations.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not trust an unchecked elimination result.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding only one term from each equation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Elimination uses the entire left and right sides.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiplying only one side during scaling.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It changes the equation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply every term on both sides.

SummaryPoints: Elimination and substitution can agree.
Choose the simpler algebraic route.
Check the original equations.

Visuals.Title: Check the difference constraint
Visuals.Description: All listed pairs sum to 7, but only (4,3) also has x−y=1.

Lessons.Title: Writing Systems of Equations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: translate a two-condition real-world situation into two equations with shared variables and clearly defined units.
Define each unknown before composing equations. A total gives a sum equation; a price or rate condition gives a second independent equation. The pair solves only when both pieces of information hold.

Invent a ticket scenario with adult tickets $8, child tickets $5, 10 tickets total and $65 total revenue. Write two equations and discuss physical restrictions to nonnegative integers. Teacher review is needed for variable definitions and consistency of the story.

Independently authored Edulytiks Grade 8 content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/4/15/preparation.html . No original publisher figures or assessments are duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Total-count condition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A sum of quantities equals known count.

KeyConcepts.Title: Total-value condition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply each count by its per-unit value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Discrete domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: Counts are nonnegative whole numbers.
KeyConcepts.Example: Five adults and five children is possible.

WorkedExamples.Title: Write ticket system
WorkedExamples.Question: Ten tickets total, adult $8 child $5, revenue $65. Define equations.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a and c as counts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject infeasible count
WorkedExamples.Question: A proposed solution has 12 adults and −2 children but sums to 10. Is it acceptable?
Steps: Negative child ticket count is impossible.
The solution is invalid for the context.
WorkedExamples.Check: Ticket counts must be nonnegative integers.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using one variable for different quantities.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Counts need distinct definitions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accepting a negative ticket count.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Algebraic solutions may violate realistic constraints.

SummaryPoints: Define variables and units.
Use independent count and value conditions.
Check both equations and practical domains.

Lessons.Title: Solving Problems with Systems of Equations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: solve contextual systems, compare feasible solutions, and interpret results including units and reasonableness.

Set up both constraints, select a solution method, and validate the final pair against every condition. If a model permits fractions but the situation requires counts, only integer nonnegative solutions are feasible.

Consider a mixture of apples and pears: eight fruits total, apples $2 each, pears $3 each, total cost $19. Determine both counts and explain why each condition matters. Teacher review checks context and reasoning.

KeyConcepts.Title: Independent constraints
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two equations simultaneously describing one situation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Eliminate a variable
KeyConcepts.Definition: Combine equations or substitute.

KeyConcepts.Rule: Check nonnegative integer counts and amounts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fruit mixture
WorkedExamples.Question: Eight fruits, apples $2, pears $3, total $19. Find counts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check alternate guess
WorkedExamples.Question: Could 4 apples and 4 pears meet both conditions?

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve a second cost system
WorkedExamples.Question: Six items total, $3 and $5 types, total cost $24. Find quantities.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring the total count after solving a cost equation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One constraint alone leaves multiple possibilities.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Giving fractional item counts without context.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Discrete objects require integer solutions.

SummaryPoints: Systems combine independent real constraints.
Solve algebraically and validate context.
A complete answer states quantities and units.
